stories.title: Officials told to strictly follow election code

article_sentences: Tirupati Municipal Commissioner M Jayakrishna instructed election officials to conduct municipal general elections with full transparency and strict code compliance.

Tirupati: Municipal Corporation Commissioner M Jayakrishna has directed officials to conduct the corporation’s general elections with utmost care, transparency and impartiality, strictly following the election code and all related rules.
Addressing Returning Officers and Assistant Returning.
Officers at a meeting here on Wednesday, the Commissioner said election code came into force and must be observed from filing of nominations until completion of the election process.
He instructed all officials to avoid errors and discharge their duties in accordance with the State Election Commission’s guidelines.
Jayakrishna asked officials at nomination reception centres to remain alert and handle the nomination process carefully, while directing Presiding.
Officers to read the relevant rulebooks thoroughly and ensure that no mistakes occur during nominations.
He also stressed the need for close coordination among officials at every stage of the election.
Additional Commissioner Sarada Devi, Deputy Commissioner Amaraiah, Bharat Naik, SE Syam Sundar and Tahsildar Suresh Babu attended the meeting.

stories.headline: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.title: NC manifesto hangs in balance as CM Omar-led govt completes 2 years in office tomorrow
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 14: They say – there’s many a slip between the cup and the lip! “Red letter day” of October 16 is just round the corner- precisely just a day away – when the incumbent elected government, led by the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, will complete its second year in office in the Union Territory set-up of Jammu and Kashmir. So here comes the perfect appraisal time to count those slips between the “cup” and the “lip”, though not in proverbial dimensions. In the context of appraisal, “lip” will denote promises by the helmsmen and “cup” – their delivery to “the ruled”. It’s time to measure and judge to what extent “Dignity, Identity and Development” promised as a “solemn pledge” to the people reached their doorsteps. If one goes by the shriller voices in the corridors of power, statehood has remained the dominant chorus – the fulcrum of the ruling alliance of National Conference-Congress’ political juggernaut throughout the year. The plank continued to offer as an impenetrable shield to the alliance and particularly the National Conference against the opposition’s unrelenting onslaught. Unlike his reconciliatory approach during the first year in office, second year saw CM Omar stridently fighting, protesting for restoration of statehood and projecting that its (statehood’s) absence only caused all the “slips” between the “cup” and the “lip” to blunt opposition’s offensive vis-à-vis non fulfilment of poll promises (by NC). Interestingly, the government, fully aware of harsh realities of politics, during its second year in power, has less relied on its trite plank during first one year that its mandate to fulfil poll promises is for five years and not one, two or three years - to duck prickly queries of both the opposition and the people. As a sagacious old player in the political arena, it has focussed more on “absence of statehood” to shift the burden of its “complete failure in governance”, (as alleged by its detractors), on its political opponents (read BJP only) as well. But does it convince the opposition, which has already written off the NC-led alliance government as “Failed” consecutively in its second Annual Performance Report (APR) or the people – the ruled? Absolutely not – in case of opposition! In the case of people, nothing can be said with certainty as they actually speak only after five years through votes! To be fair, it (NC government) has tried to take baby- steps towards the realisation of several of its promises made in its manifesto. Though it’s a story for another day that most of those steps, so far, have proved to be nothing more than paper-horses – the distance between the cup and the lip persists. Keeping the “paper-horses” proposition in mind, one can tick mark the boxes while sifting through its 12 guarantees, as mentioned in NC manifesto 2024. With regard to its first guarantee related to “Restoration of political and legal status” – it continues to strive for “full implementation of autonomy resolution”; “restoration of Articles 370 and 35 A” and statehood as prior to August 5, 2019. The government has kept its promise – it is striving for all three “big guarantees.” But how will it continue to strive for them? None has any idea and even the government, itself, is clueless. In any case, except statehood, two other guarantees can justifiably be not part of the government's real APR (other than the wordy duel). However, it kept its word to move resolutions in the assembly and get them passed. While it succeeded in reviving its autonomy resolution of 2000 in the just concluded autumn session of J&K Legislature, the words Articles 370 and 35-A could not see their verbatim entry in any of resolutions passed so far by the House or the J&K Council of Ministers. Cornered by the opposition in this context, the government maintained that the word “special status” mentioned in the resolutions was their (Articles 370 n 35-A’s) cloak. It had promised to make endeavours to redraw the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 and the transaction of Business of the Government of Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir Rules, 2019. As promised, its endeavours continued even when it’s about to complete its second year in office. “Files remained pending with the Centre,” the government reaffirms. The status of files related to tweaking of reservation rules (policy), committee report about regularisation of daily wagers too remains in knowledge of government only. Opaqueness persists about the efforts to “modify, annul and repeal post August 5, 2019 laws impacting J&K’s special status”; “protect the land and employment rights of the people of J&K” and “secure the release of prisoners languishing in jails.” But as they are some tricky propositions, it will be fair enough to push their APR to 2029. Similar is the status about the guarantee to repeal the Public Safety Act (PSA). One can wait for these guarantees to fructify, even after 2029. But the opposition and people can genuinely question the status of guarantee to “fill up all vacancies in government departments within 180 days” and realisation of other related promises on the ground (beyond announcement and flurry of paper horses). Next guarantee related to “200 units of electricity free”. In the manifesto, there were no strings attached to it. But in the current scenario, as opposition, too, repeatedly targets – the government has shifted its “goal post to AAY families” and now it is linked to “PM Surya GharMuftBijliYojana” of Government of India. Moving on, does anyone remember that the party has given a guarantee to “provide Rs 5000 per month to female heads of EWS households”? If not, forget it. EWS (families) to get 12 cylinders free of cost per year - was another guarantee. The government, in its second year, endeavoured to fulfil this promise partially and with “strings attached.” It has kept its promises to enhance the old age and widow pension, free ride for women (with partial tweaking) in e-buses and free education (for all) with a tweaked proposition. It has been successful in restoration of Darbar Move in its second year. The government has maintained that it has also fulfilled its poll promise related to “Ease of Doing Business” with the passage of a related bill in the just concluded autumn session. Rest of its major guarantees and promises remain out of its own realm so far and this gives the opposition a handle to beat it, in an unrelenting manner. “How dual power is creating obstruction in good governance? On statehood, earlier NC (other parties’) stance was - it would come on its own and we will have to wage a bigger war for Art 370 and 35 A. Youth continue to be incarcerated in jails outside J&K. What has happened to 12 free cylinders to all? There were certain achievable goals even within the UT setup, they (NC government) could not get them even,” maintains former minister and senior leader of J&K Apni Party, G H Mir, while talking to GKTV. He claimed that in 1983, NC in its manifesto had promised to ensure posts for Chief Secretary, DGP and Chief Justice for J&K citizens but after coming to power, it brought Chief Secretary from outside. “When there was statehood, they wanted autonomy. In the current scenario, they are seeking statehood. It simply means they don’t want to deliver. We too support statehood demand. But their (NC’s) politics always revolves around exploitation of people’s sentiments by provoking them against the Centre and not good governance. They are now resorting to confrontational politics. Confrontation is not going to help it, anyway. It did not help in the past, it will not help even now,” Mir points out. “The election happened under the UT setup to govern a Union Territory. The Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, himself, was on record saying that he had served as the Chief Minister of State so it would be embarrassing for him to contest for power in UT. But he did and won power. However, he could not effectively use powers even within the UT set up to make people’s life better. Dual power is a system prevalent at many places but it cannot be used as an excuse to deprive the people of good governance or one promised to them (people) while contesting for UT. How is the dual system obstructing filling of vacant posts,” former minister argues. Leader of the Opposition in J&K Legislature Sunil Sharma too has repeatedly targeted the government for using “statehood” as a plank to “cover-up its failure to fulfil poll promises.” “Corruption has become deeply entrenched under the present dispensation, while transparency and accountability have been completely sidelined. The government's policy of outsourcing jobs without establishing a transparent and foolproof recruitment mechanism,” he alleges, adding, “Such policies created ample space for manipulation, favouritism and corruption while depriving deserving youth of fair employment opportunities.” J&K BJP leadership also criticises NC government, for what it alleges, “deliberately resorting to dirty tactics to delay Panchayat elections, weaken the Panchayati Raj Institutions and obstruct the functioning of the three-tier democratic system in Jammu and Kashmir.” “The grassroots democracy could not be sacrificed for political convenience,” BJP leaders assert.

stories.headline: India’s business transformers: Leaders driving growth, innovation and sustainable change
stories.title: India’s business transformers: Leaders driving growth, innovation and sustainable change
stories.summary: Hemant Malhotra — Group COO, Venture CatalystsWith more than 24 years of experience in building, scaling and turning around global business services organisations, his mandate at Venture Catalysts spans operations, customer experience, risk and exits across seven group companies—the breadth of a CEO’s desk.His career includes leadership roles with Smith & Nephew, JLL, Genpact/GE and Worley, where he has owned P&Ls exceeding $125 million and led multi-geography teams of more than 3,000 people. People management and change management have remained defining strengths throughout his career, particularly across transitions and transformations in CPG, manufacturing, media and banking.At Venture Catalysts, he brings a data-driven, AI-first mindset to identifying, managing and exiting startups across the portfolio. He has been instrumental in designing the TM AI engine and a lean, multi-fund operating model that translates data and a sharp understanding of the startup ecosystem into earlier signals, better decisions and stronger investor IRR with greater predictability. His approach reflects the strategic ownership and P&L orientation of a leader positioned for a larger-organisation CEO mandate. Babita Spinelli — CEO, Babita Spinelli GroupAn award-winning psychotherapist, global speaker and executive coach, her work sits at the intersection of psychology, business and human transformation. Her distinctive career spanning law, Wall Street and Big Four consulting gives her a multidimensional perspective on the complexities facing today’s executives and professionals.Her work focuses on human behaviour and emotional intelligence, helping leaders globally navigate high-pressure environments, strengthen self-awareness, break limiting patterns and lead through change with greater clarity and confidence. Her approach extends beyond traditional executive development, examining the psychological and emotional dynamics that influence decision-making, relationships and professional impact.Her insights have been featured in prominent business and media outlets. Through her work, she continues to advance a more human-centred approach to success—one that connects emotional intelligence, resilience and personal transformation with meaningful and sustainable impact. Silvester Stalin — Director, VerosCertFor startups and growing businesses, compliance can open doors to enterprise clients, tenders and international markets. Yet many face a gap between low-cost services centred on obtaining a certificate and comprehensive consulting engagements priced beyond their reach.VerosCert, a division of Veronikas Creatives Pvt. Ltd., was established to bridge this gap by making practical, implementation-focused compliance support more accessible. Its services span ISO standards—including ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 22301, ISO 27001, ISO 42001 and ISO 45001—alongside SOC 1 and SOC 2 readiness, CMMI, PCI DSS, cybersecurity compliance and process improvement.Each engagement begins with understanding how the organisation operates. VerosCert then guides teams through gap assessment, documentation, implementation, training and internal audits, while coordinating with independent certification and attestation bodies. The emphasis is on building systems that teams can use and maintain in their everyday work.Since beginning operations in 2024, VerosCert has supported organisations across diverse industries, including a public sector undertaking early in its journey. It has expanded its presence to the Philippines and Saudi Arabia, and recently opened in Singapore, extending its support to businesses across these markets.By combining accessible pricing with hands-on guidance, VerosCert helps emerging organisations meet enterprise expectations and strengthen their operations. Its aim is to make compliance a lasting business capability—one that supports customer trust, market access and sustainable growth.https://veroscert.com Shrikant Sarda — Chief Strategy Officer, Growth Sense; Co-founder & CTO, Target PEAKWith more than three decades of experience as a business strategist and technology leader, his work has focused on helping organisations pursue long-term strategic growth and navigate technology-led disruption.A firm believer that technology should be viewed not as a cost item but as a strategic growth lever, particularly for MSMEs, he works closely with board members, MSMEs and startups to formulate growth, cost and operational transformation strategies. His experience includes senior leadership roles with global IT services organisations, including Managing Director at Accenture Technology and Practice Head at Wipro Technologies.Today, his leadership portfolio spans Growth Sense Group, Target PEAK and strategic advisory roles with several SME companies.His vision is to make best-in-class strategic advisory services accessible to MSMEs and startups at an affordable cost, enabling them to approach technology and transformation as drivers of sustainable growth rather than merely operational necessities. Devasani Sreenivas — Director, Prowealth FinvestSuccessful investing begins not with a product, but with understanding the investor. Every individual and family has distinct financial goals, responsibilities, risk preferences and time horizons, making a thoughtfully structured investment approach essential to a long-term wealth journey.Prowealth Finvest focuses on helping clients understand and access suitable mutual fund and other permitted investment products, with an emphasis on appropriate asset allocation, diversification and periodic portfolio reviews. Through market understanding, transparent communication and personalised engagement, the firm seeks to help investors make better-informed investment choices while maintaining perspective beyond short-term market movements.A key pillar of the philosophy is investor behaviour. Particularly during periods of market volatility, discipline, patience and clear communication play an important role in helping investors maintain a long-term perspective.Built on trust, transparency and enduring relationships, Prowealth Finvest continues to strengthen its technology-enabled service capabilities while preserving personalised engagement. The firm seeks to remain a dependable financial distribution partner throughout an investor’s wealth journey.Devasani Sreenivas | Prowealth Finvest Private LimitedAMFI Registered Mutual Fund Distributor Ashish Vilasrao Gawhane — Director, Vevra PackagingAt the convergence of packaging, logistics, technology and sustainability, Vevra Packaging is emerging as a differentiated supply-chain solutions platform.With four manufacturing units, 11 warehouses, more than 153 employees and over 100 customers, the company has established a scalable operating footprint across India’s key industrial corridors. Its integrated portfolio spans returnable transport packaging, rental pooling, expendable packaging, onsite packaging with automation, reverse logistics, asset management and transportation.This integrated model enables customers to reduce capital intensity, improve asset productivity and build more resilient supply chains. Its strength lies in an asset-light, consultative and technology-enabled approach that combines engineering capabilities with operational execution and recurring-service opportunities.As manufacturers increasingly prioritise cost optimisation, traceability and circularity, Vevra is positioning itself to capture this shift with a platform designed for scale, recurring revenue and long-term customer integration. Its proposition extends beyond packaging to the continuous optimisation of the supply chain itself. Aniruddha Nene— Founder and CEO, One SG TechnologiesFollowing his graduation from IIT Bombay, he began his entrepreneurial journey with a medical imaging startup and later led a landmark three-way merger that created one of India’s early consolidated healthcare informatics companies.Recognising the transformative potential of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) amid the post-pandemic digital shift, he founded One SG Technologies in 2024. The company believes that India needs a patient-centric and interoperable care ecosystem and is working to bridge gaps in connected healthcare through its flagship interoperability platform, OneHCX®.A key focus is addressing the complexity and unpredictability of medical claim outcomes, particularly against the backdrop of inadequate health coverage and the resulting friction between payers and providers. AI-powered OneHCX® has been extensively trained and matured within the Insurtech sector, offering interoperability, regulatory compliance and AI co-piloted digital claims processing capabilities for care providers and beneficiaries.Through this approach, the company aims to create a more seamless connected-care experience while enabling sustainable adoption across the healthcare ecosystem.The pages slugged ‘Brand Connect’ are equivalent to advertisements and are not written and produced by Forbes India journalists.

stories.headline: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.title: Historic Shah Kul: HC seeks updated report on demarcation, removal of encroachments
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 14: The High Court of J&K and Ladakh has granted the authorities 10 more days to complete the ongoing demarcation and removal of encroachments from the Shah Kul -- a historical canal of importance and a national monument that had been the main source of water to Nishat Gardens since the time of Mughal Emperor Jahangir. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri directed the authorities to submit a report updating the status of demarcation and removal of encroachments on the Shah Kul by October 27. The Court was hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by Mir Muhammad Shafi in 2023, seeking restoration of the centuries-old canal and removal of encroachments from its original alignment. During the proceeding, the court’s attention was drawn to the divisional commissioner Kashmir’s status report indicating constitution of a committee comprising the Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar; Vice Chairman, Lakes Conservation and Management Authority (LCMA); Regional Director, Survey and Land Records (Central), Srinagar; and Superintending Engineer, Irrigation and Flood Control, Srinagar. The committee formed pursuant to the September 15 order, has been tasked with consolidating the list of encroachments after proper demarcation with reference to revenue records, examining claims regarding property rights and preparing a time-bound action plan for removal of identified encroachments and restoration of Shah Kul. The Court was informed that the demarcation exercise had commenced and that voluntary removal as well as time-bound removal of encroachments was being undertaken simultaneously. It was also told that around 47 structures broadly fell within the scope of encroachment. Of these, 28 structures have so far been demarcated, while around 20 have already been removed. The remaining eight demarcated structures are likely to be removed shortly, they informed the court. Furthermore, the authorities further submitted that once the demarcation exercise is completed, any encroachers who fail to remove the structures voluntarily would face removal during an anti-encroachment drive. Allowing the 10-day time sought by them, the Bench directed the authorities to update the Court on the progress made in the demarcation and removal exercise.

stories.headline: Khadi and Village Industries: Weaving the Fabric of Inclusive and Sustainable India
stories.title: Khadi and Village Industries: Weaving the Fabric of Inclusive and Sustainable India
stories.summary: We are proud citizens of India -today the sixth largest economy in the world in terms of nominal GDP. Much of the economic growth is driven by the MSME sector contributing one-third in the overall GDP of the country. Herein again, major share comes from rural micro enterprises. The rural economy mainly relies on cottage industries like Khadi and handloom sector along with handicraft products manufactured from rural artisans. At a time when the world is grappling with inequality, climate change and resource depletion while in the domain of IT and software, AI is on relentless march gobbling up jobs, Khadi and Village Industries (KVI) can play an important role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and strengthening the vision of an Atmanirbhar Bharat by enabling employment at differential skill levels, with low resource use locally mitigating migration too. Khadi, Hand spun and Hand woven, has been the Soul of Bharat. The responsible production is resource efficient on energy, water utilising natural fibres. The potential to be the driver of growth is being recognised steadily, albeit, slowly. Our industry signifies a rich cultural legacy from ancient times, exhibiting a diverse artistic sense with exemplary skill and personal touch of human emotions. Various written treatise pertaining to the Rigveda, Ramayana, Mahabharata, Thalia (by Greek historian Herodotus) and Kautilya have mentioned not only spinning and weaving but also the high quality of silk and cotton. While cotton has been cited in Ramayana and aligned to characteristics of Saint, the spectrum of weaves reflect the rich cultural tapestry. Through Khadi ‘Production by Masses’ using hand spun and hand woven, was utilised by Mahatma Gandhiji to confront Mass production by the Colonialists. The fabric of freedom is becoming aspirational fashion statement today because of its unique characteristics of being natural, comfortable and sustainable. Its handmade character gives it an individuality and hence it does not need to compete with generic production in volumes. The journey of Khadi—from a symbol of swadeshi and freedom to a contemporary fashion and lifestyle choice especially for environmentally aware new generation —demonstrates how tradition can adapt to changing consumer preferences. In fact, Tradition of near source production, which is more sustainable, is by default, intrinsic strength in Khadi ecosystem. In 21st Century, KVIC takes inspiration in our mandate from the clarion call of Hon’ble Prime Minister, “Khadi for Nation, Khadi for Fashion and Khadi for Transformation” while contributing to farm, fibre and market connect. It has to be noted that Hand spinning is the cardinal differentiator between Khadi and Handlooms. Since Yarn is also done by hand, the labour-intensive nature production enables employment to large section of people. The Khadi institutions, the aggregators of the hand-made hank produced in distributed architecture, have been assisted by Khadi and Village industries over last seven decades. Capacity enhancement through Skilling and up-skilling is being done through KVIC’s departmental and non-departmental training centers. With two-third of the rural population in the country, this sector holds larger significance as it provides ample opportunities for rural entrepreneurs. Such interventions directly advance SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by creating income-generating opportunities for people at the grassroots. Recent measures, including increases in spinning and weaving wages from April 2025 by Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), incremental support to improving working tools, conditions, tools infra, marketing interfaces, further demonstrate the emphasis on improving artisan incomes and making traditional livelihoods attractive and economically sustainable. The aggregate production has reached ~Rs 4000 crore(approx.) with Sales reaching about Rs 8000 crore(approx.) due to constant strengthening of the Khadi and Village industries (VI) Ecosystems over period, especially last one decade. Marching forward, the comfort fabric has been evolving into new categories and aspirational statements. Its transformation is evident in the emergence of Khadi denim, designer saris and bridal wear, contemporary shirts and trousers, and collections by mainstream brands such as Raymond and Peter England. Centre of Excellence for Khadi (NIFT, Delhi), an initiative between Ministry of MSME and Textiles, has developed 2129 Khadi design collections in the multiple categories of apparels, collections of home-made-ups, featuring prints, weaves, embroidery, and painting, sari designs and continues to enable the Khadi Institutions/ aspirants through CoEK knowledge portal. Our foray into infant wear is inspired by the fact that global infant and baby wear segment is expected to be exceeding $60 billion by 2030 (CAGR between 5-8.1%) and there would be priority to organic cotton, hypoallergenic fabrics and non-toxic manufacturing processes. Navyug Khadi designs reflecting positioning of Brand for 21st Century India, launched at National Crafts Museum & Hastkala Academy, Pragati Maidan with 710 new products presenting the “New Khadi of New India” in a contemporary and innovative manner along with Khadi Knowledge Portal. A collection of Wellness/Yoga wear ‘Svadha’ has been recently launched on International Yoga Day to attract all age groups from Gen Z to young at heart. Employment generation in Khadi requires very low investment. The assistance is being provided through schemes viz. Khadi Vikas Yojana, Gramodyog Vikas Yojana, PMEGP enabling KVI institutions/units in providing employment opportunities. The government is giving a major push to revive traditional industries by providing them all the necessary support including financial assistance, working capital facilitation, quality raw material support training, tool-kits, wage compensation, marketing support, promotion of digital payments and social security benefits. As per the evaluation study conducted by EDII, Ahmedabad, in its report submitted in January, 2026, over 75% of artisans across all the schemes reported a measurable increase in income post-intervention and a stable year-round employment was created for artisans who previously depended on seasonal or migratory labour which actually helped in reducing the migration of labour. Artisans trained under food processing, agarbatti, and Honey Mission have diversified into new product categories—such as essential oils, scented candles, or value-added honey derivatives. This diversification has improved resilience against local market fluctuations. Khadi directly addresses women’s empowerment and hence aligns to Inclusive development. Around 80 percent of around half a million Khadi artisans are women. Female participation was found to be dominating in GVY schemes, particularly in Agarbatti, Handmade Paper, Honey Mission, and Service Industry segments according to the study. Therefore, the engagement of a large number of women in any capacity in this sector has ensured direct remunerations for them, thus empowering them through financial independence and improved self-worth both within and outside of their homes. By enabling women to participate in productive economic activity, Khadi contributes directly to SDG 5 (Gender Equality) while also helping reduce social and economic disparities under SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). The handmade industry has a growing global demand and huge export potential which needs to be tapped. With its quantum and varieties of traditional handmade products, India occupies an inevitable place in the world. 85% of the global handloom production occurs here and the ‘intrinsic value’ can be leveraged for ‘higher returns’. Other handloom nations like Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia manufacture very limited range of products but these are mainly for domestic production. India has the huge potential to cater to the global demand of Khadi and handloom products based on its demographic advantage and diversified cultural heritage. Consumers around the world are showing growing interest in products that are handmade, traceable, natural and environmentally responsible. This presents an opportunity to reposition Khadi and handmade products not merely as traditional goods, but as premium products that embody authenticity, strong backstory of craftsmanship and sustainability. KVIC has got registered as EPC on the Trade portal of Consulate General of India at New York, USA under Ministry of External Affairs. KVIC has initiated registering the progressive KIs with EXIM licenses and also engaging with Consulates in India for exposures to our strengths, which should enable building bridges. While Khadi has its recognition, the Brand is being protected through registering trade Mark in other countries so that our producers and value chains are protected. Further unique Branding, Geographical Identification (GI) tag has been recently awarded to Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) in respect of Ponduru Khadi which will enhance its value realisation for products of unique cotton and products spun and woven through equally unique process. The inaugural BRICS MSME Forum held in Agra this year exhibited specialized and premium products, including GI-tagged Ponduru Khadi, Bharat Kasturi Cotton, Bengal Muslin and naturally coloured cotton products. We need to ensure Quality and assurance in our products for enhancing new gen Z customer acquisition, retention and higher value returns for such niche products . Towards this end, the department's Central Sliver Plant (CSP), established nearly three and a half decades ago, are being modernized. Of the five currently operational CSPs, the plants located in Chittaradurga, Karnataka, and Kuttur, Kerala, have completed modernization and are operational. The Sliver plant in Karnataka utilises Solar energy for 50% of the requirement while wind power is being explored to make the production totally environmentally supportive. This approach resonates with SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) by connecting traditional enterprises with design, technology, modern markets and evolving supply chains. Technology Up-gradation of Khadi Institutions’ Production Infrastructure and technology-based Common Facility Centres (CFCs) are proposed to strengthen Village Industries clusters through shared infrastructure and modern processing facilities. KVIC is enabling Traceability solutions across the value chains which should enable integrating IT to tradition and attract new gen interest in the production ecosystem also. Last but not the least, the cottage industry is eco-friendly in nature being energy efficient, water efficient and use of natural fibres/ colours . Khadi is an eco- friendly fabric with very less carbon footprint and environmentally sustainable. The measurement of this is being studied by premier Institutions (IIT, IIMs) to enable suitably factoring in the product as well as Brand promotion narrative to agile new gen consumer – domestic and international. The focus of the world economies has recently shifted towards taking initiatives with a more pragmatic approach in ensuring development that has social and environmental connotations alongside economic growth. The ethical aspects of materialistic expansion have drawn attention of the policy makers in the wake of alarming environmental concerns, rising inequalities, hunger and poverty and inequitable distribution of resources. The 2030 agenda for Sustainable Development with its 17 goals adopted by World nations in 2015 underline the course of action for achieving the development based on poverty eradication, judicious use of environmental resources, and distributive social justice. KVIC in collaboration with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Central Institute for Research on Cotton Technology (ICAR-CIRCOT), is actively exploring initiatives aimed at developing naturally coloured cotton varieties. This approach aligns with eco-friendly practices by minimizing water usage, chemical pollution, and energy consumption associated with traditional dyeing processes. It would be therefore pertinent to give impetus to this sector which has the capacity to provide sustainable livelihood solutions. At a time when the fashion industry is under increasing pressure to address waste, pollution and excessive resource consumption, Khadi offers an alternative philosophy; produce thoughtfully, consume responsibly and value the skill behind every product. In fact, whatever fibre or filament, by nature (eg plastic wrapper) and / or length (eg desi cotton) cannot be converted to Yarn by mechanised spinning industry, can be done through hand charkha and can enable ‘in loop’ as well as ‘ out of loop’ recycling and upcycling and thereby contribute to additional employment categories in hand spinning. This directly connects Khadi with SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action). Sustainable agricultural practices, including responsible cotton cultivation, can further strengthen its contribution to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 15 (Life on Land) by promoting more sustainable rural ecosystems. With these potential, constant support and promotion would keep making the supply chains stronger, deeper and wider in delivering responsibly to human society. The larger message is simple; sustainability, need not always come from the newest technology only. Sometimes, it can emerge from practices that communities have preserved for centuries that modern society is rediscovering. Khadi represents precisely such a possibility. It combines heritage with innovation, employment with entrepreneurship, women’s empowerment with social inclusion, and economic activity with environmental responsibility. We, at KVIC, are trying to uncover, demystify, reassert and reinforce that MAGIC woven by Artists of Threads, our spinners and Artisans, for the environmentally conscious world. (Ms. Roop Rashi is Chief Executive Officer, KVIC & Dr. Nitesh Dhawan is Dy. CEO, KVIC, Mumbai. Courtesy: PIB)

bullets.text: Centre of Excellence for Khadi (NIFT, Delhi), an initiative between Ministry of MSME and Textiles, has developed 2129 Khadi design collections in the multiple categories of apparels, collections of home-made-ups, featuring prints, weaves, embroidery, and painting, sari designs and continues to enable the Khadi Institutions/ aspirants through CoEK knowledge portal.

sentences.text: Recent measures, including increases in spinning and weaving wages from April 2025 by Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), incremental support to improving working tools, conditions, tools infra, marketing interfaces, further demonstrate the emphasis on improving artisan incomes and making traditional livelihoods attractive and economically sustainable.

Navyug Khadi designs reflecting positioning of Brand for 21st Century India, launched at National Crafts Museum & Hastkala Academy, Pragati Maidan with 710 new products presenting the “New Khadi of New India” in a contemporary and innovative manner along with Khadi Knowledge Portal.
Female participation was found to be dominating in GVY schemes, particularly in Agarbatti, Handmade Paper, Honey Mission, and Service Industry segments according to the study.

The aggregate production has reached ~Rs 4000 crore(approx.) with Sales reaching about Rs 8000 crore(approx.) due to constant strengthening of the Khadi and Village industries (VI) Ecosystems over period, especially last one decade.

stories.headline: The Himalayas Cannot Be Developed Into Submission
stories.title: The Himalayas Cannot Be Developed Into Submission
stories.summary: The Lieutenant Governor’s call for a comprehensive, science-based and people-centric approach to mountain development comes at a time when the Himalayan region can no longer afford the luxury of delay. Across Jammu and Kashmir, the signs of ecological stress are visible in shrinking water sources, unstable slopes, erratic weather, forest degradation, unplanned construction and the growing vulnerability of settlements to disasters. The crisis is no longer theoretical. It is increasingly shaping the lives and livelihoods of mountain communities. The message delivered at the Sustainable Mountain Development Summit correctly places the Himalayas at the centre of India’s environmental and developmental concerns. These mountains are not merely scenic landscapes or tourism destinations. They are the source of rivers, reservoirs of biodiversity and natural regulators of climate. Any disturbance to their ecological balance carries consequences far beyond the immediate location of the damage. Yet, the central challenge lies in translating a sound vision into enforceable action. For decades, development in the mountains has often been pursued through a plains-based model—wider roads, larger buildings, expanding towns and rising tourist numbers—with insufficient regard for the region’s fragile carrying capacity. Roads are carved into unstable slopes, construction continues along water channels and flood-prone areas, and waste accumulates in places that lack the infrastructure to manage it. Such development may produce short-term economic gains, but it deepens long-term public risk. The proposed emphasis on science-based carrying capacity and zoning is therefore fundamental. No town, valley or tourist destination should be permitted to grow beyond what its water, land, drainage, waste-management and emergency systems can sustain. Carrying-capacity assessments must not remain policy language confined to summit documents. They must determine where construction is allowed, what kind of infrastructure is suitable and how many visitors a destination can safely accommodate. Climate-resilient infrastructure is equally urgent. Mountain roads, bridges, buildings and public facilities must be designed for local terrain and changing weather patterns. Modern technology can improve forecasting and early-warning systems, but it must work alongside the knowledge of communities that have lived with the mountains for generations. Local experience can often identify the first signs of a landslide, flood or water crisis long before formal systems respond. The focus on regenerative livelihoods offers another important direction. High-value horticulture, organic farming, sericulture, eco-tourism and other green enterprises can reduce pressure on fragile ecosystems while creating opportunities for youth and women. But this requires access to markets, credit, training and reliable infrastructure. Empowerment cannot be reduced to slogans; it must be supported by sustained institutional investment. The proposed zero-waste and circular mountain economy must also become a public priority. Tourist destinations and urban centres cannot continue generating waste without adequate systems for segregation, recycling, sewage treatment and scientific disposal. The Himalayas do not need development at any cost. They need development that understands limits. Tradition and technology, economic ambition and ecological restraint must move together. The true measure of a developed region will not be the height of its buildings or the number of tourists it attracts, but whether its rivers flow, its slopes remain stable, and its people can live securely within the limits of nature.
